challenges.headline: "Edit the total" as a direct write
challenges.premise: The request treats editing a reported total as a normal field edit.
challenges.alternative: In this domain a total is derived from underlying entries; corrections are usually modeled as an auditable adjustment entry, not a direct overwrite of the aggregate.
challenges.consequence: A silent override decouples the report from its own source data — the classic way a financial report stops tying out, discovered at audit time rather than build time.
challenges.recommendation: Confirm with Finance whether the edit must be an adjustment entry (visible, reversible, attributed) before any data model is built.

challenges.headline: No period-close boundary
challenges.premise: The request implies totals can be edited whenever a user wants to.
challenges.alternative: Closed periods are normally frozen; a correction after close is a restatement or a next-period adjustment, not an edit to the closed figure.
challenges.consequence: Without this boundary, someone will eventually 'fix' a closed, filed period directly — invalidating everything already exported or reported from it.
challenges.recommendation: Define the period lifecycle and the allowed edit path at each stage before scoping the edit feature.

challenges.headline: No segregation of duties
challenges.premise: The request names 'users' who edit and 'the finance team' who receives figures, with no distinction between who edits, approves, or closes.
challenges.alternative: This domain treats editor, approver and period-closer as three distinct rights, often for compliance reasons (the person adjusting a figure shouldn't be the one closing the period).
challenges.consequence: Skipping this now means retrofitting roles and approval gates after acceptance testing, when it's most expensive to add.
challenges.recommendation: Settle the permission model — who edits, who approves, who closes — as part of initial scoping, not after build.
